blocks.text: After at least k arrivals, the smallest value among the retained k largest values is exactly the kth-largest answer. A max-heap of all history can answer but retains unnecessary information, while FIFO order ignores value rank.

blocks.text: A min-heap maintains exactly the ordering needed at the root while allowing insertions and removals without re-sorting the entire waiting set. The task does not require every job to be globally ordered; it requires the next smallest deadline again and again. A one-time final ordering favors sorting, membership favors a set or map, and strict arrival order favors a queue. Transfer this rule to any workload that repeatedly exposes one best candidate under updates.

blocks.text: Within a sorted source, no later value can precede its current head. Therefore the next global output must be the smallest among the current heads, and after one head is emitted only that source advances. The heap stores the frontier rather than all N values. If sources are not sorted, this frontier proof fails; if there are only two sources, a direct two-pointer merge may be simpler.

This yields O(N log k) merge time for N total values and k sources, rather than repeatedly sorting all remaining values.

blocks.text: Initialize `smallest` to the first array value, scan each remaining value once, and replace `smallest` whenever a lower value appears. This takes `O(n)` time and `O(1)` auxiliary space. Sorting takes `O(n log n)` comparison time, and a balanced tree maintains substantially more order than one answer requires. The boundary changes when later operations repeatedly insert candidates or remove the current extreme.

blocks.text: Changing a key in place can violate both parent and child heap relations. An indexed heap can sift the updated entry, while lazy versioning can insert a new version and discard stale roots before peek or pop. Without one of these contracts, the root may represent an obsolete priority and no longer be the current best job.

blocks.text: A standard heap efficiently repairs order when the changed entry is known, but it does not by itself provide constant-time lookup of an arbitrary job. The design may keep an index from job ID to heap position, use an indexed priority queue, or insert a new version and discard stale entries when they reach the root. The repeated-extreme signal therefore survives, while the mutation contract determines the supporting state. If updates disappear, a simpler ordinary heap may be enough.

messages.text: Changing priorities do not replace the priority contract with arrival order; the next job is still selected by an extreme key.
Heap order does not provide direct lookup by arbitrary job ID. Updating an unknown interior entry requires additional indexing or another validity strategy.

prompt: A scheduler repeatedly removes the smallest current priority, but an already queued job may later receive a new priority. Which diagnosis is most precise?

items: Priority dispatch keeps a heap ordered by the scheduler's declared priority comparator, so the best waiting task is at the root and arrivals update the frontier.
K-way merge keeps one head from each nonexhausted sorted source in a min-heap; emitting the minimum advances only its source and inserts that source's next head.
Streaming kth-largest keeps a min-heap of the `k` largest values seen so far; its root is the smallest retained value and therefore the current kth largest once at least `k` values have arrived.

blocks.text: A one-time membership test is a lookup problem, and a one-time complete ordering is a sorting problem. Surface words such as “largest” or “sorted” are not enough; the decisive structure is repeated extreme selection from a changing candidate set.
